title: What you will be able to do
instruction: Press reveal to see each outcome for this lesson.

_items.text: Apply critical thought to the choices you make when searching, reading and planning, not only when writing.

title: Being critical before you write a word
body: Being critical is usually framed as something you do to a finished source: you read it, then judge it. But the habit starts earlier than that, in the choices you make while deciding what to search for, what to read, and what to trust before you have written anything at all.

title: Opening up the discourse
body: Dennis and Abbott (2026, pp.117-118) put the goal plainly: 'When beginning your research, therefore, your goal should be to open up the relevant discourse.' That means your first search should deliberately widen what you see, not just confirm what you already expected to find.

title: Worked example
body:
Consider two students starting the same piece of coursework.

{{learner-a}} searches a topic, keeps the first three results because they are easy to find, and starts writing from those alone.

{{learner-b}} searches the same topic, but deliberately varies the search terms to surface more than one position, and only then decides which sources to trust.

Both searched. Only {{learner-b}} opened up the discourse before settling on a view.

title: Why this counts as being critical
body: Nothing here is about reading more. It is about noticing that the first search result is one voice in a discourse, not the whole of it, and choosing to look for the other voices before you decide what you think.

title: Search choices checklist
body: Use these questions before you commit to a set of sources.
instruction: Tick each item once you have tried it.

_items.text: Did I write down the scope of the question before searching?
Did I note which sources I will trust, and why?
Did I vary my search terms rather than using the first ones I thought of?
Did I flag any assumption built into how the question was framed?

title: Order the search steps
displayTitle: Put the search steps in order
body: These four steps describe a critical approach to starting a search, but they are out of sequence.
instruction: Drag items to reorder, or use the keyboard (Enter to grab, arrows to move, Enter to drop). Then select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Put the four search steps in order, from first to last.

_items.text: Scope the question before searching anything.
Note which sources you will trust and why.
Flag any assumptions built into what you find.

_feedback.correct: That is the right order. Scoping and noting trusted sources come before you search, varied terms open up the discourse, and flagging assumptions comes once you have something to question.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what has to be decided before you search, and what can only happen once you have results to look at.

title: Doing this in practice
body: Before you collect anything, write down the scope of your question, the sources you expect to trust, and any assumption you can already see in how the question is framed. This takes minutes, and it changes what you end up reading.

title: Your turn
instruction: This is for your own reflection; no right answers are expected.

_items.text: Think of a recent piece of work. Did your search open up the discourse, or did it confirm what you already expected?
What is one search term you could add next time to deliberately surface a different position?
